1. Acid Secretion Physiology, GERD and PUD

Drug classesDr. Waller picked no prototype drugs: you must be able to recognize and categorize all of them. Three categories: (1) agents that reduce gastric acidity: proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), the potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB), histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs), antacids; (2) mucosal protective agents; (3) antibiotic therapy for Helicobacter pylori. Red in this guide marks the drugs and regimens she spends the most time on.

Physiology of acid secretion

  • Gastrin (from antral G cells) is the most potent inducer of acid secretion. It acts mainly indirectly: binds CCK-B receptors on enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells → histamine release → histamine binds H2 receptors on parietal cells (Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA) → activates the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump). A lesser direct effect on parietal cells also exists.
  • Acetylcholine (ACh) from vagal postganglionic nerves binds parietal M3 muscarinic receptors (Gq → PLC → IP3 → Ca2+) for potent direct stimulation; it also binds ECL cells to release histamine.
  • Somatostatin (antral D cells) inhibits acid secretion by suppressing gastrin: gastric pH <3 triggers its release (negative feedback).
  • Prostaglandins E2 and I2 inhibit the pump by lowering cAMP (EP3 receptors, Gi) and stimulate mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow. NSAIDs block prostaglandin production → more acid, less mucus and bicarbonate, less blood flow: ulcerogenic.
  • Two major antisecretory drug sites: the histamine H2 receptor and the proton pump.
Physiology of acid secretion (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Gastric secretion and sites of drug action (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

  • Symptoms or complications from reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus or beyond. Nonerosive vs erosive disease (by endoscopy), which affects therapy.
  • Classic: heartburn, regurgitation, chest pain. Atypical: dyspepsia, epigastric pain, nausea, belching. Extraesophageal: asthma, chronic cough, laryngitis.
  • Alarm symptoms (need endoscopy): bleeding, anemia, early satiety, unexplained weight loss, progressive dysphagia, recurrent vomiting, family history of GI cancer, prior esophagogastric malignancy.
  • Causes: transient LES relaxation, reduced LES tone, delayed gastric emptying, pregnancy hormones. Complications: erosive esophagitis, stricture, Barrett metaplasia (small adenocarcinoma risk).

Peptic ulcer disease (PUD)

  • Mucosal damage from pepsin and acid in the stomach (gastric) or proximal duodenum (duodenal). >90% are from H. pylori infection or NSAID use; others: stress-related mucosal injury (poor perfusion in the critically ill), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrin-producing tumors).
  • Ulcers arise when aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, bile) overwhelm defensive factors (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, blood flow).
  • Symptoms: burning epigastric pain after meals or on an empty stomach; classic duodenal ulcer pain 2–5 hours after a meal and at night (11 pm–2 am) relieved by food. Some are silent and present with hemorrhage or perforation.

Therapeutic goals

Relieve symptoms, heal ulcers, prevent recurrence and complications (hemorrhage, perforation), reduce aggressive factors, maintain gastric pH >4, eradicate H. pylori if present, increase protective factors (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins).

Lifestyle modification (GERD)

Target populationModification
Overweight/obese or recent weight gainWeight loss
Nocturnal symptomsAvoid meals 2–3 hours before bed; left-side sleeping; elevate head of bed
Tobacco usersSmoking cessation (lowers LES tone)
Identified triggersAvoid caffeine, coffee, chocolate, spicy/acidic/high-fat foods only if symptoms improve

2. Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)

Agents: omeprazole (Prilosec, Zegerid), esomeprazole (Nexium), pantoprazole (Protonix), rabeprazole (Aciphex), lansoprazole (Prevacid), dexlansoprazole (Dexilant). All oral; only pantoprazole and esomeprazole also come intravenous (IV). At equivalent doses, little difference in efficacy.

PPI mechanism (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Mechanism and pharmacokinetics

  • Irreversibly (covalently) inactivate the H+/K+-ATPase: the final common pathway of acid secretion; they inhibit both fasting and meal-stimulated secretion (90–98% of 24-hour acid).
  • Inactive prodrugs; lipophilic weak bases that diffuse into the acidic parietal cell canaliculus, are protonated and trapped (>1000-fold concentration), converted to the active sulfenamide, which forms a disulfide bond with cysteine on the pump.
  • Delayed-release, enteric-coated to protect the acid-labile prodrug; dissolves in the alkaline small intestine.
  • Food decreases bioavailability (~50%): give on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before a meal (breakfast); PPIs only inhibit actively secreting pumps.
  • t½ ~1.5 hours but acid inhibition lasts 24 hours (irreversible; new pumps take ≥18 hours to be made). Needs 3–4 days for full effect and 3–4 days for acid secretion to return after stopping: not for “on-demand” use.
  • Rapid first-pass and hepatic metabolism (CYP2C19 and 3A4); negligible renal clearance.

Uses

  • GERD (erosive and nonerosive, stricture, Barrett, extraesophageal); PUD (faster relief and healing than H2RAs); H. pylori eradication (minor antimicrobial effect; raising pH lowers antibiotic MICs); NSAID ulcers (required if the NSAID must continue); prevention of rebleeding; Zollinger-Ellison; over-the-counter (OTC) short-term frequent heartburn.
  • Stress-related mucosal injury: omeprazole sodium bicarbonate is the only PPI approved (via tube in ICU patients); without a nasoenteric tube, IV H2RA is preferred over IV PPI.

Adverse effects and interactions

TopicKey points
Common ADRs (1–5%)Diarrhea, headache, abdominal pain (only slightly above placebo)
Safety concernsClostridium difficile (2–3x risk); ↓ vitamin B12 absorption; nosocomial pneumonia; modest hip fracture risk; small enteric infection risk. Use the lowest effective dose for the appropriate duration
Altered absorptionLess acid → ↓ absorption of ketoconazole, itraconazole, atazanavir (need acid); digoxin levels may rise
CYP interactionsRare (short t½); omeprazole may inhibit metabolism of warfarin (↑ INR), diazepam, phenytoin, methotrexate. Pantoprazole and rabeprazole: no significant interactions
ClopidogrelFDA warning: clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole may reduce its antiplatelet effect. If co-administered, prefer pantoprazole or rabeprazole

3. Potassium-Competitive Acid Blocker (P-CAB): Vonoprazan

Agent: vonoprazan (Voquezna), the newest agent.

P-CAB mechanism (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
  • Mechanism: competitive, reversible inhibition of the potassium-binding site of the H+/K+-ATPase; blocks both active and inactive pumps, so K+ cannot reach the pump.
  • No acid activation needed → rapid, potent suppression from the first dose; effective fed or fasted; maximal effect in 1 day (vs 3–5 days for PPIs); good nocturnal acid control; concentrates in parietal canaliculi more than PPIs.
  • PK: peak 0.5–2 hours; long t½ ~7.9 hours; metabolized by CYP3A4/5 (not CYP2C19), so less interindividual variability than PPIs.
  • Uses: erosive and nonerosive GERD (esp. LA grade C/D), PUD healing and prevention, NSAID/aspirin gastric protection, H. pylori combination therapy, on-demand therapy for intermittent heartburn.
  • ADRs: generally well tolerated: diarrhea, nasopharyngitis, dyspepsia, headache, abdominal pain. DDI: strong CYP3A4/5 inhibitors or inducers.
  • Cost may be prohibitive, so PPIs and H2RAs are still compared most.

4. Histamine-2 Receptor Antagonists (H2RAs)

Agents: cimetidine (Tagamet), famotidine (Pepcid), nizatidine (Axid; prescription only), ranitidine (Zantac; withdrawn in 2020 because of contaminant levels that rise over time and may increase cancer risk).

H2RA mechanism (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
  • Mechanism: competitive inhibition at parietal cell H2 receptors (highly selective; no H1 or H3 effect). Blocks histamine released from ECL cells, but ACh and gastrin still act directly on the parietal cell.
  • PD: suppress basal and nocturnal acid (histamine-dependent) well; only a modest effect on meal-stimulated acid. Nocturnal control is the most important determinant of duodenal ulcer healing, so evening dosing.
  • PK: bioavailability ~50%; t½ 1–4 hours but duration is dose dependent (6–10 hours); dose-reduce in renal (and severe hepatic) impairment. Potency varies 50-fold but all are about equally effective at usual doses.
  • Uses: intermittent heartburn or dyspepsia (<3x/week; heavily OTC); occasional duodenal ulcers; IV H2RA preferred for stress-related mucosal injury without a nasoenteric tube.
  • Tolerance: reduced effect with repeated dosing (within ~3 days). No tolerance with PPIs (site is distal to histamine).
ADRs (<3%)Details
CommonDiarrhea, headache, fatigue, myalgia, constipation
Mental status changesConfusion, hallucinations, agitation, especially IV in ICU, elderly, renal or hepatic dysfunction
CimetidineInhibits dihydrotestosterone binding to androgen receptors, inhibits estradiol metabolism, raises prolactin: gynecomastia or impotence in men; galactorrhea in women
OtherNosocomial pneumonia; rare blood dyscrasias (thrombocytopenia); bradycardia/hypotension with rapid IV infusion (give over 30 minutes)

Drug interactions

  • Cimetidine inhibits CYP1A2, 2C9, 2D6, 3A4 (cimetidine » ranitidine; famotidine and nizatidine negligible): ↑ theophylline, warfarin, phenytoin, lidocaine (narrow therapeutic index).
  • Cimetidine competes with creatinine and procainamide for renal tubular secretion. All H2RAs except famotidine inhibit gastric first-pass metabolism of alcohol.

Rebound dyspepsia and acid hypersecretion can follow stopping either PPIs or H2RAs.

Antacids

Agents: sodium bicarbonate (baking soda, Alka-Seltzer), calcium carbonate (Tums, Os-Cal), magnesium hydroxide/aluminum hydroxide (Mylanta, Maalox). Weak bases that react with HCl to form a salt and water, neutralizing acid; fast, cheap, OTC; used for dyspepsia and intermittent heartburn.

Antacids (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
AntacidReactionProblems
Sodium bicarbonateHCl → NaCl + CO2 (rapid)Gastric distention, belching; metabolic alkalosis; Na+/fluid retention (heart failure, hypertension, renal insufficiency); not long term
Calcium carbonateHCl → CaCl2 + CO2 (slower)Belching, metabolic alkalosis; with dairy: hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency (milk-alkali); not long term
Mg(OH)2/Al(OH)3HCl → MgCl2 or AlCl3 + H2O (no gas)No belching, alkalosis uncommon. Magnesium: osmotic diarrhea; aluminum: constipation (combined to balance). Avoid long term in renal insufficiency

DDI: antacids bind drugs and change pH: do not give within 2 hours of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and iron. Sodium alginate (seaweed polysaccharide) forms a floating foam barrier between gastric contents and the gastroesophageal junction. Muscarinic antagonists modestly reduce acid but need doses with too many adverse effects.

6. Clinical Pharmacology: GERD

Empiric treatment (no endoscopy)

SymptomsApproach
Mild, intermittent (<2 episodes/week)Lifestyle modification + as-needed antacids or low-dose H2RAs. If persistent: twice-daily H2RA or switch to once-daily PPI (step-up approach)
Frequent or severe (≥2 moderate-to-severe episodes/week)Standard-dose PPI once daily + lifestyle for 8 weeks. Vonoprazan is an alternative if no response to PPIs

Endoscopy-guided

  • Erosive esophagitis (Los Angeles B–D): vonoprazan daily for 8 weeks is preferred (superior healing); PPIs reasonable if cost is a concern.
  • Barrett esophagus, strictures, anatomic abnormalities: individualized.

Pregnancy or breastfeeding

  1. First line: lifestyle + as-needed antacids or sucralfate (1 g orally three times daily). Antacids are generally safe, but avoid sodium bicarbonate and magnesium trisilicate (sodium bicarbonate: metabolic alkalosis and fluid overload; magnesium: fetal effects with long-term high doses). Sucralfate is likely safe (minimal absorption).
  2. If persistent: add H2RAs (safe).
  3. Still uncontrolled: PPIs: omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole preferred; low breast milk secretion and likely degraded in the infant's stomach.

7. Clinical Pharmacology: PUD

  • All patients: test and treat for H. pylori; withdraw offending factors (NSAIDs).
  • All receive antisecretory therapy, typically a PPI; PPIs are preferred over H2RAs (faster symptom control, higher healing rates, better in NSAID ulcers). H2RAs are occasionally used for duodenal ulcers (nocturnal acid). Vonoprazan is an alternative (rapid onset, longer duration, potent).
Ulcer typeTreatment
H. pylori-positivePPI + antibiotics for 14 days; no extra PPI needed unless symptoms persist; eradication alone heals >90% of duodenal ulcers
NSAID-inducedPPI for 4–8 weeks (by size); if the NSAID must continue, maintenance daily PPI (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg)
Idiopathic (no H. pylori, no NSAID)PPI 4 weeks (duodenal) or 8 weeks (gastric); repeat endoscopy for gastric ulcers before stopping; may need long-term PPI
Complicated (bleeding, perforation, penetration, gastric outlet obstruction)High-dose PPI (twice daily), then once daily after 4 weeks; 4–8 weeks duodenal, 8–12 weeks gastric, with endoscopic confirmation of healing before stopping
PregnancyPPI (lansoprazole or pantoprazole preferred); H. pylori eradication usually deferred until after delivery (bismuth, fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines are not recommended; clarithromycin, amoxicillin and probably metronidazole are low risk, especially after 14 weeks)

9. Helicobacter pylori Infection and Combination Therapy

  • Spiral, gram-negative rod; ~50% of the world is infected. Most common cause of PUD.
  • Test when: active PUD (regardless of NSAID use), past documented ulcer never treated for H. pylori, gastric MALT lymphoma, or a “test-and-treat” approach for uninvestigated dyspepsia in patients <60 years old with no alarm features.
  • Goal: heal the ulcer and eradicate the organism. The first course is the best chance; previous antibiotic exposure lowers success. Use proven regimens, the right duration, stress compliance, counsel on adverse effects.
  • No single drug is adequate: PPI (± bismuth subsalicylate) + two or more antibiotics for 10–14 days. PPIs help by a minor direct effect and by raising pH (lowering antibiotic MICs). Choose by local resistance, prior antibiotics/allergies, cost and preference.
AntibioticAdverse effects
AmoxicillinGI upset, headache, diarrhea
ClarithromycinGI upset, diarrhea, altered taste
MetronidazoleMetallic taste, dyspepsia, alcohol intolerance
TetracyclineGI upset, photosensitivity
H. pylori first-line regimens (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Traditional regimens (kept for board-style questions)

Triple therapyBismuth quadruple therapy (preferred)Concomitant therapy
PPI (BID) + clarithromycin (BID) + amoxicillin (BID) or metronidazole (TID)PPI (BID) + tetracycline (QID) + metronidazole (QID) + bismuth subsalicylate (QID)PPI (BID) + clarithromycin (BID) + amoxicillin (BID) + metronidazole (BID)

Triple and concomitant therapy have declined in efficacy from clarithromycin (macrolide) resistance; use only with no prior macrolide use in an area of low resistance.

Current first-line options (treatment-naive adults)

RegimenDetails
Optimized bismuth quadruple therapy (BQT)First-line empiric therapy in North America: PPI standard dose BID + bismuth subsalicylate QID + tetracycline QID + metronidazole 3–4x daily; 14 days. Pylera (bismuth subcitrate + metronidazole + tetracycline capsules) + PPI: 10 days
Rifabutin-amoxicillin-PPI triple (Talicia)Combination capsule (omeprazole 40 mg, rifabutin 50 mg, amoxicillin 1 g), 3x daily, 14 days; preferred over components (consistent intragastric levels, less rifabutin exposure). Rifabutin is on the WHO watchlist: use cautiously (resistance, tuberculosis-endemic regions)
Vonoprazan-amoxicillin dualVonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1 g 3x daily, 14 days (Voquezna Dual Pak)
Vonoprazan-amoxicillin-clarithromycin tripleVonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg BID, 14 days (Voquezna Triple Pak); only with confirmed clarithromycin susceptibility
Penicillin allergyThe rifabutin and vonoprazan regimens both contain amoxicillin, so a confirmed penicillin allergy needs a different approach. Alternative first-line regimens are considered where BQT eradication falls below 85%. You need to recognize an appropriate regimen, not design one.
